passage: The prize distribution at the school hall in Indore ran late because the sound system kept crackling. Rukmini, five, walked back from the stage with her medal, chest out, chin up, marching like a soldier. Her father Kamal, holding a cold drink, clapped. On the way out, a group of older children crowded near. Rukmini's chest sank, and she stepped behind Kamal's leg, holding the medal against her tummy. He said quietly, "You can show them when you're ready." After a minute, she peeked out and held the medal up.

qa.q: What did Rukmini do with her chest when she walked back from the stage?
qa.a: She walked back with her chest out and her chin up.

qa.q: What does Rukmini's stepping behind her father's leg suggest she felt when the older children crowded round?
qa.a: It suggests she felt shy or wary, since her chest sank and she held the medal to her tummy. She might also simply have been tired after the long event.

qa.q: What could Kamal do to help Rukmini in a crowd?
qa.a: He can let her take her time behind him and invite her to show the medal when she is ready, as he did.

qa.q: How might the older children see Rukmini's marching walk?
qa.a: They may see a proud small girl, and might not realise she felt shy when they crowded round.

grounding: A preschooler shows pride through posture and shrinks when shy, and a gentle warm-up time helps.

passage: After scoring at the colony's cricket match, Sunaina, six, stood tall by the wicket, hands on hips, shoulders back, grinning at her father Vikas at the boundary. "Did you see?" she called. "I saw!" he said. Then a tall neighbour boy asked her to bat again in front of the whole crowd. Her shoulders rounded and her hands went to her sides. She looked at Vikas. "Maybe later," he told the boy. Sunaina smiled and sat down beside him, relaxed.

qa.q: Where was Vikas when Sunaina scored?
qa.a: He was at the boundary.

qa.q: What does Sunaina's change of posture suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: Standing tall with hands on hips suggests pride in her score. Rounded shoulders and looking at her father suggest she felt shy or under pressure when asked to bat in front of the crowd.

qa.q: What could Vikas do to support Sunaina's shyness?
qa.a: He can do as he did, protecting her from the pressure and letting her decide when she is ready to perform again.

qa.q: How might the neighbour boy feel when Sunaina doesn't bat again?
qa.a: He may feel a little let down, but he may also have just wanted more of the fun.

grounding: Posture shows pride after a success and shyness under pressure, and a shy child needs warm-up time.

passage: When the harvest festival drums began in the village near Nashik, Madhuri, five, dropped her spoon and started to spin, her scarf flying out, arms up. She clapped in circles and stamped her feet, laughing out loud. Her aunt Gurpreet, carrying a tray of sweets, put it down and joined, clapping the beat. Madhuri giggled harder and pulled her aunt's hand. Later, her legs shaky and her breathing quick, she flopped onto the mat, still smiling, and said, "More!"

qa.q: What did Madhuri drop when the drums began?
qa.a: She dropped her spoon.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling as she spun and clapped?
qa.a: She was full of joy at the music, since she laughed out loud and pulled her aunt's hand. Her movement may also have been a way to release her excess energy.

qa.q: Why was it helpful that Gurpreet put down her tray and danced?
qa.a: Joining in showed Madhuri that her delight was welcome and made them closer, more than praising or correcting would have done.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet feel when Madhuri pulls her hand to dance?
qa.a: She may feel warm and happy, and glad she stopped what she was doing to join her niece. 😊

grounding: A preschooler spins and claps for joy at music, and joining in strengthens bonding.

passage: At the football club's trophy day in Durban, Thabo, four, jumped up as the announcer called out his team's win. He stomped, shook his arms and did a wobbly dance beside his older brother Siddiq. Siddiq laughed and copied, wiggling his hips. Thabo shrieked, then ran a circle round the chairs, and his flushed face beamed. When Siddiq scooped up the small trophy, Thabo dashed back and spun once more. Their mother filmed them from the seats, smiling but not saying a word.

qa.q: Who called out the team's win?
qa.a: The announcer called out the win.

qa.q: What might Thabo have been feeling as he stomped and danced?
qa.a: He was probably thrilled about the win, and his flushed, beaming face and shrieks show delight. Running circles may also have been him letting off a rush of energy.

qa.q: What could Siddiq do that helps his brother enjoy the moment?
qa.a: He can keep joining in the dance, as he already did, instead of telling Thabo to sit down.

qa.q: How might their mother feel watching them?
qa.a: She may feel happy and proud, and choose to enjoy the moment without interrupting it.

grounding: A preschooler dances and celebrates a win, and a sibling joining in shares the joy.

passage: Playground note by Farida, nursery helper. At the games corner, Nandini lost the ring-toss to a classmate. She dropped the last ring, turned her back and walked to the far fence, arms stiff. I noticed she kept looking at the game from a distance. I didn't follow. After a few minutes I called, "Nandini, we'd like you back for the next round if you want." She waited, then came back and stood at the edge before rejoining. I think she was upset and needed a little time, though she may also have been embarrassed.

qa.q: What game did Nandini lose?
qa.a: She lost the ring-toss to a classmate.

qa.q: What might Nandini have been feeling when she turned her back and walked to the far fence?
qa.a: She was probably upset or embarrassed about losing, and needed space. She kept looking back at the game, which suggests she still wanted to be part of it.

qa.q: What did Farida do that gave Nandini space without pushing her away?
qa.a: Farida didn't follow, then invited Nandini back with a calm call and left the choice to Nandini.

qa.q: How might the classmate who won see Nandini walking off?
qa.a: They may feel confused or a bit guilty, unless an adult explains that Nandini just needs a moment.

grounding: A child walks off after a lost game, and a calm invitation to return works better than following with demands.

passage: In the hill village of Mizoram, Lalremsiami, five, was told off for taking her cousin's slate and she turned to the wall. Then she walked out, past the shoes at the door, and sat on the step by the chickens. Her grandmother Damini stayed inside stirring the pot, and watched through the doorway. After a few minutes she called softly, "The rice is ready when you are." Lalremsiami stayed a bit longer, then wandered in, and leaned on Damini's knee without a word.

qa.q: Where did Lalremsiami sit after walking out?
qa.a: She sat on the step by the chickens.

qa.q: What might Lalremsiami have been feeling when she turned to the wall and walked out?
qa.a: She may have felt embarrassed or upset about being told off and wanted space. She might also have felt cross that she was told off.

qa.q: Why did Damini stay in the kitchen and call softly?
qa.a: She gave Lalremsiami room to calm down and a way back without demanding an apology, and Lalremsiami came in on her own.

qa.q: How might the cousin see Lalremsiami walking away?
qa.a: The cousin may think she is angry or feel a little guilty, and would understand better if someone explained she wanted space.

grounding: A young child walks off after a rebuke, and a calm invitation to return works better than following with demands.

passage: The siren from the sugar factory near Kolhapur wailed at noon, and Nikita, five, pressed both hands over her ears and squeezed her eyes shut. Her mother Tanuja, who was chopping onions in the doorway, saw her daughter's shoulders hunch. She put down the knife, walked over and said, "That's loud, isn't it? Let's go inside where it's quiet." They sat on the cool floor behind the curtain. When the siren stopped, Nikita lowered her hands slowly and said, "It's gone."

qa.q: What did Nikita do when the siren wailed?
qa.a: She pressed both hands over her ears and squeezed her eyes shut.

qa.q: What might Nikita have been feeling as the siren wailed?
qa.a: She was probably overwhelmed and frightened by the loud noise, and her hunched shoulders show she was trying to protect herself. She may also have found it just too loud.

qa.q: What did Tanuja do that helps Nikita learn that limits are allowed?
qa.a: She respected the covered ears, named the noise as loud and took Nikita somewhere quieter.

qa.q: How might Tanuja have felt watching her daughter cover her ears?
qa.a: She may have felt protective and concerned, and put down her knife to help straight away.

grounding: A preschooler covers her eyes and ears when input is too much, and a quieter space teaches that limits are allowed.

passage: In a cinema in Seoul, a dragon roared on the big screen. Rania, four, slid down in her seat and pulled her jacket hood over her eyes, fingers pressed against her ears. Her father Jin whispered, "Do you want to step outside for a bit?" Rania nodded. In the lobby, she sipped water, her hands dropping from her ears. "Too loud," she said. Jin nodded. "Too loud. We can go back or stay here. You choose." She thought and said, "Stay."

qa.q: What did Rania pull over her eyes?
qa.a: She pulled her jacket hood over her eyes.

qa.q: What might Rania have been feeling when the dragon roared?
qa.a: She was likely frightened or overwhelmed by the noise and picture, since she slid down and covered her eyes and ears. She might also just have found it too loud.

qa.q: What could Jin do next time Rania finds a film too much?
qa.a: He can offer a break as he did, and let her choose whether to go back, so she learns that limits are allowed.

qa.q: How might Jin feel when Rania covers her eyes and ears?
qa.a: Jin is probably concerned for her and wants to help, which is why he quietly offers to step outside instead of telling her to keep watching.

grounding: A preschooler covers her eyes and ears when the input is too much, and a quiet space teaches that limits are allowed.

passage: I was in the courtyard of our block in Hyderabad when a visiting uncle bent to hug Rafiq, six, who stiffened and ducked away, arms crossed over his chest. The uncle laughed, "Come on, one hug!" Rafiq shook his head. "No hug." His mother Jahnavi stepped in. "He said no. Would a high-five do?" The uncle held up his palm and Rafiq slapped it, looking relieved. I couldn't tell if he was tired, shy or just didn't want to be touched, but his body was clear.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do when the uncle bent to hug him?
qa.a: He stiffened and ducked away, with his arms crossed over his chest.

qa.q: What did Rafiq's body suggest about how he felt, and what does the narrator say they couldn't tell?
qa.a: His stiffening and ducking suggest he was uncomfortable with the hug, and his relief at the high-five fits that. The narrator couldn't tell whether it was tiredness, shyness or not wanting to be touched.

qa.q: What can Jahnavi do to support Rafiq?
qa.a: She can keep respecting his signals and offer other ways to greet, such as a high-five, and encourage him to say no or tell a trusted adult if he is pressured.

qa.q: How might the uncle feel when Rafiq ducks away?
qa.a: He may feel a little rejected, but the high-five lets him greet Rafiq without making it about him.

grounding: A child pulls away from an unwanted hug, a valid signal that caring adults respect.

passage:
Day one: at the aunts' gathering in Dhaka, Zeenat, five, pulled back when a relative reached to pinch her cheek. Her mother Dilnaz said, "She'd rather wave." Zeenat waved.
Day three: at the park, a neighbour tried to lift Zeenat onto a swing. She stiffened, and Dilnaz said gently, "Zeenat, do you want help?" Zeenat shook her head and climbed herself.
Day six: Zeenat told her mother, "I don't like when they pinch. I can say no." Dilnaz hugged her, asking first.

qa.q: What did Zeenat do when the relative reached to pinch her cheek?
qa.a: She pulled back.

qa.q: What does Zeenat's stiffening on day three suggest about her feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she felt uncomfortable about being lifted without asking. Her calm headshake and climbing by herself show she preferred to decide for herself.

qa.q: What could Dilnaz keep doing to help Zeenat with saying no?
qa.a: She can keep noticing her signals, speaking up for her when needed and praising her words, and tell her to speak to a trusted adult if pressure continues.

qa.q: How might Zeenat feel on day six when her mother asks before hugging her?
qa.a: She may feel her body is her own and trust her mother more.

grounding: A child pulls back from touch she doesn't want, and adults respect it while she learns to say no.

subtype: Covering the mouth when shy or surprised [Expressing]
passage: At the picnic in a Buenos Aires park, Pablo, five, kicked the ball at his friend Jamal and accidentally hit the water bottle, which rolled into the pond. "Oops!" Pablo clapped his hand over his mouth, wide-eyed. Jamal's shoulders shook. Then his hand flew up over his own mouth, and the two of them dissolved into giggles behind their fingers. Pablo's mother, standing beside the blanket, smiled at them, and Pablo peeked at her face, then lowered his hand.

qa.q: Where did the water bottle roll?
qa.a: It rolled into the pond.

qa.q: What might Pablo have been feeling when he clapped his hand over his mouth?
qa.a: He was probably surprised and a little embarrassed about the slip. He may also have found it funny, since he later giggled behind his fingers.

qa.q: How could Pablo's mother help him feel safe after a slip like this?
qa.a: A gentle smile and reassuring words help him see it was only an accident, as her smile did.

qa.q: How does Jamal seem to see Pablo's mistake?
qa.a: He finds it funny and joins in, covering his mouth to laugh with Pablo.

grounding: A child covers his mouth after a slip in giggles and shy surprise, and a gentle smile helps him feel safe.

subtype: Covering the mouth when shy or surprised [Expressing]
passage: Group time at a Lucknow school. Ira, the teacher, held up a picture of a giant tortoise, and Aadhya, five, gasped and covered her mouth with both hands, eyes shining. Then Ira asked the class who could name the animal. Aadhya's hand went to her mouth again, and she looked at the floor. "Tortoise," she whispered through her fingers. "Yes!" said Ira warmly, smiling. Aadhya lowered her hand a little, and gave a small smile back.

qa.q: What did Aadhya do when she saw the picture of the tortoise?
qa.a: She gasped and covered her mouth with both hands.

qa.q: What could Aadhya's hand over her mouth mean on the second occasion?
qa.a: It probably showed shyness about speaking up in front of everyone, and the first time it seemed to show awe. Her whisper and looking down support shyness.

qa.q: How does Ira's smile help Aadhya?
qa.a: It tells Aadhya her answer was welcome and that it is safe to speak, so she smiles back.

qa.q: How might the other children see Aadhya's hand over her mouth?
qa.a: They may think she is giggling or hiding something, and might not realise she is shy.

grounding: A child covers her mouth in awe and in shyness, and context and a gentle smile help.

passage: Rehana's daughter Zainab, five, sat in the doctor's waiting room in Ahmedabad, chewing her thumbnail and picking at her frock. The receptionist called other names. Rehana noticed. "You're nervous, aren't you?" Zainab nodded slowly. "Let's breathe like we do at bedtime: smell the flower, blow the candle." They did it together three times, quietly. Zainab took her thumb from her mouth and said, "Will it hurt?" Rehana answered honestly, "The doctor will tell us what she's doing."

qa.q: What was Zainab chewing in the waiting room?
qa.a: She was chewing her thumbnail.

qa.q: What does Zainab's thumb-chewing and picking suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she was nervous about seeing the doctor, and she nodded when her mother asked. It could also have been simply waiting that she found hard.

qa.q: What did Rehana do that worked better than a scolding?
qa.a: She named the nervousness and taught a calming breath they did together, without telling Zainab off for chewing.

qa.q: How might Zainab feel when her mother says the doctor will tell them what she's doing?
qa.a: She may feel a little more prepared and less alone, though she still might be a little worried.

grounding: A preschooler nail-bites and picks at clothes when nervous, and deep breaths work better than punishment.

passage:
"Kunal, take your finger out of your mouth."
"I'm not."
"You are, and you're picking your shirt."
"I'm waiting."
"For what?"
"For my turn on the trampoline." Kunal's shoulders were stiff.
Bhavna knelt. "Waiting is hard. Do you want the squishy star to squeeze while you wait?" Kunal took the star from her bag and squeezed it. "Better?" "A bit." "Let's count the bounces together." His fingers stayed out of his mouth.

qa.q: What was Kunal waiting for?
qa.a: He was waiting for his turn on the trampoline.

qa.q: What does Kunal's biting and picking suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he was nervous or impatient about waiting for his turn, since his shoulders were stiff. He said only that he was waiting.

qa.q: What worked in Bhavna's approach?
qa.a: She didn't punish him and gave him a squishy star to squeeze and a counting game, which gave his fingers something else to do.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel if Bhavna had just told him off?
qa.a: He might feel ashamed and still be nervous, without a better way to cope.

grounding: A preschooler picks and bites when waiting, which is self-soothing, and a fidget object helps more than punishment.

passage: Our neighbour in the Chandigarh lane, Maria, had her mother-in-law staying, and I was at their door when the older woman said to Maria's four-year-old, Nilufar, "Give Dadi a kiss." Nilufar hid behind her mother's leg. I saw Maria crouch. "You can choose. A kiss, a hug, a wave or a high-five?" Nilufar peered out. "Wave." She waved. Her Dadi nodded and waved back, smiling, though her face fell a little. I don't know whether Nilufar was tired or shy, but she looked easier after that.

qa.q: What options did Maria give Nilufar?
qa.a: She offered a kiss, a hug, a wave or a high-five.

qa.q: What might Nilufar have been feeling when she hid behind her mother's leg?
qa.a: She may have felt shy or simply didn't feel like being kissed. The narrator can't be sure whether she was tired or shy.

qa.q: What could Maria do to help her daughter and Nilufar's Dadi?
qa.a: She can keep offering choices and explain to Dadi that a wave is welcome too, so that everyone feels respected.

qa.q: How might Nilufar's Dadi feel when Nilufar waves instead?
qa.a: She may feel a bit disappointed at first, which shows in her face, but she still smiles and waves back.

grounding: A preschooler learns that hugging or kissing is a choice, and accepting a wave teaches that her body belongs to her.

passage:
Day one: at a family party in Coimbatore, Keerthana, five, was asked to hug her uncle. She shook her head and held out her hand. Her father Sahil said, "A handshake is fine."
Day four: her cousin asked, "Can I have a hug?" Keerthana said, "Yes," and they hugged.
Day seven: her grandmother arrived and said, "Come!" Keerthana said, "Can we do a high-five?" Grandmother grinned, and they slapped hands.

qa.q: What did Keerthana offer her uncle instead of a hug?
qa.a: She held out her hand.

qa.q: What does Keerthana's yes on day four suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she was happy to hug her cousin because she was asked first. Her shake of the head on day one shows she can decide for herself, without meaning she dislikes her uncle.

qa.q: What should adults keep doing to protect the child's sense of control?
qa.a: They should keep asking before hugs, accept a handshake or high-five and thank the child for telling them.

qa.q: How might the grandmother feel about a high-five?
qa.a: She may be pleased that Keerthana still connects with her, and she grinned, so the high-five worked.

grounding: A preschooler learns hugging is a choice, and adults who accept a wave or high-five teach that her body belongs to her.

passage: At the community centre in Guwahati, the counsellor Bhupen held up a card in safety class. "Some touch feels comfortable, like a hug from someone you trust. Other touch leaves you scared or muddled. Your private parts are yours. Only a grown-up helping you wash, or a doctor with Mama there, may need to touch them." Sabina, five, stared, her hands very still. "If someone says it's a secret?" "Tell a grown-up you trust, like Mama, even if they said not to." "Mama," said Sabina. Later Bhupen knelt beside her. "You can come and talk to me any time."

qa.q: Who is the counsellor at the community centre?
qa.a: The counsellor is Bhupen.

qa.q: What might Sabina have been thinking when she asked about a secret?
qa.a: She seems to be trying to understand what to do if someone asks her to keep a secret, and her stillness suggests she was thinking hard about it. She may also have felt unsure or a little worried.

qa.q: What message should the child take from the class?
qa.a: If a touch ever feels bad or someone says to keep it secret, Sabina should tell a grown-up she trusts, like Mama or Bhupen.

qa.q: How might Sabina's mother feel when Sabina tells her what she learned?
qa.a: She may feel glad that her daughter knows who to tell, and she can listen calmly and take her seriously. 🤍

grounding: A child learns that safe touch feels comfortable, unsafe touch feels scary, and secrecy is a signal to tell a trusted adult.

passage: I help at the after-school club, and I overheard Shankar, six, talking to his friend by the water cooler. "My cousin's friend touched me where he shouldn't. It felt yucky. He said it's a secret." Lokesh stood still. "Secrets like that aren't okay. That's what Ms Bindu told us. Tell a grown-up." I walked over and knelt beside them. "Thank you for telling me, Shankar. You did the right thing, and it's not your fault." I stayed with the boys and asked another helper to fetch the head teacher straight away.

qa.q: Who said that secrets like that aren't okay?
qa.a: Lokesh said that Ms Bindu told them so.

qa.q: What might Shankar have been feeling when he said it felt yucky?
qa.a: He seemed uncomfortable and confused about what happened, and worried about the secret. He may also have feared he would get in trouble.

qa.q: What should an adult do when a child tells them about unsafe touch?
qa.a: Stay with the child, listen calmly, say it is not their fault and send someone to fetch the head teacher that same day so the child is protected.

qa.q: How might Lokesh feel when he tells his friend to speak up?
qa.a: He may feel worried for Shankar and a bit unsure, but he remembers what he was taught.

grounding: A child recognises unsafe touch and secrecy, and a trusted adult responds by listening and getting help.

passage:
"Not so close, Harish," said Parul, laughing, at the bus stop in Surat. Harish, five, leaned right into her face to show a beetle in his palm.
"It's big!"
"It is! But let's take one step back so I can see it. About an arm's length." She stretched out an arm. Harish stepped back until his fingers nearly touched it.
"Like that?"
"Perfect. Grandma gets a closer look though, right?"
"Yes, Grandma gets a hug." He grinned, and went to find the beetle a leaf.

qa.q: What was in Harish's palm?
qa.a: There was a big beetle in his palm.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling as he leaned into Parul's face?
qa.a: He was probably excited and eager to share his discovery, which is why he got so close. He probably wasn't trying to bother her.

qa.q: What made Parul's way of teaching personal space work?
qa.a: She explained it kindly with an arm's length and a clear example, and said some people such as Grandma can stand closer.

qa.q: How might Parul feel when Harish leans right into her face?
qa.a: She may feel a little crowded, though she stays friendly and gives him a clear guide.

grounding: A child learns that arm's length is a fair distance for many talks and that family may stand closer.

passage: Class note by Mridul, Reception teacher in Jaipur. Sumit, five, stands very close to friends when he speaks, so close that Aarav shrinks back. Today I knelt beside Sumit and said, "Let's find the right distance. Hold out your arm. That's the space where we usually talk." Then I asked him to practise with me. He stepped back, and beamed. Later, in a crowded queue, another child, Neel, froze and clutched his bag. I've taught the class to say, "Please give me space." Neel used it, and children moved back.

qa.q: How did Mridul teach Sumit the right distance?
qa.a: Mridul asked Sumit to hold out his arm and showed him that this is the space where we usually talk.

qa.q: What might Neel have been feeling when he froze in the crowded queue?
qa.a: He was probably uncomfortable at being crowded, since he clutched his bag. He might also have been unsure how to speak up.

qa.q: What could Mridul do to keep helping both children?
qa.a: Mridul can keep practising the arm's length and the sentence "Please give me space" with the whole class.

qa.q: How might Aarav feel when Sumit stands too close?
qa.a: Aarav may feel uncomfortable and want to move away, so the clear words help Aarav too.

grounding: A child learns arm's length is a fair distance, and children who crowd or freeze need gentle coaching and clear words.
